title: Volume and frequency
summary: Weekly hard sets per muscle are the main dial for growth: more sets help, with diminishing returns. How you spread those sets across the week matters much less once the weekly total is the same, so frequency is mostly a tool for fitting volume in and keeping sessions productive.

features: Body map colours per muscle per workout (volume-model.json visuals.body_map.ramp)
Frequency notes and suggestion buttons (rules.json rules: low_frequency; suggestion_buttons)
app_link.explains: Why the board counts weekly sets per muscle, why each muscle has a minimum and a sweet spot, and how to think about one workout versus the whole week.

sections.heading: Weekly volume drives growth
body: Volume here means hard sets per muscle per week. Across many studies, more weekly sets went with more growth, but each extra set added less than the one before.
That is why each muscle has a minimum and a sweet spot rather than a single number, and why the weekly curve flattens as sets climb.

points.text: A meta-analysis found a graded dose-response: more weekly sets per muscle went with more growth, and the highest category (ten or more sets) grew most.
A larger, newer meta-regression found growth kept rising with weekly volume, with diminishing returns.
The app's per-muscle minimum and maximum are coaching choices built on these pooled findings; only a few muscles have their own dose-response data.
Past the maximum, extra sets add fatigue faster than they add growth for most people. The exact turning point is individual and not measured.
Beginners usually grow on less volume, so their minimums and sweet spots start lower.

sections.heading: Counting indirect work
body: Compound lifts work several muscles. Counting every muscle as a full set would overstate volume; ignoring helpers would understate it.
The app gives each muscle a fraction of a set based on how much it works in that exercise.

points.text: Counting indirect sets as half a set fit the pooled growth data better than counting them fully or not at all.
The app refines this with per-exercise ratings and ignores very small ratings. The ratings are coaching estimates.

sections.heading: Frequency: how often each muscle is trained
body: Frequency is how many days a week a muscle gets meaningful work. Older analyses favoured twice a week over once, but many of the studies behind that gave the higher-frequency groups more total sets.

When studies matched weekly volume, frequency made little difference to growth. Spread sets in whatever way lets you keep every set hard; for most people that means two or more sessions for muscles with higher targets.

points.text: When weekly volume was equated, studies found no meaningful difference in growth between training a muscle more or less often. Where higher frequency did better, it was mostly because it came with more sets.
The newer meta-regression found the effect of frequency on growth was compatible with being negligible, while strength gains rose with frequency.
An earlier analysis of fewer studies favoured twice a week over once a week with volume equated; later, larger analyses did not confirm a clear difference.
Frequency helps in practice by splitting a large weekly total into sessions short enough to stay productive.
In the same analysis, strength gains rose with frequency, so training a lift more often may help when getting stronger at it is a goal.

sections.heading: How much to do in one workout
body: Within one workout, each extra set for the same muscle adds less, while fatigue keeps building. The day body map shows this as a colour for each muscle.

Dark green covers the best range in one workout, a handful of hard sets for most muscles and a little fewer for very tiring lifts. Yellow means past it; red means extra sets now cost more than they build.

Weekly sets still count in full wherever they land, so going past the per-workout cap is only an info note. Two buttons offer fixes: Make it more efficient trims or swaps past the peak, and Push for max growth adds sets up to the cap. Neither runs unless you tap it.

points.text: A large per-workout analysis found growth kept rising with more sets in a session, with diminishing returns from the first sets. It is a preprint plus a conference abstract and has not been peer-reviewed.
The colour breakpoints and the per-workout cap are coaching choices for comparing plans, not measured limits.
A note also appears when the same muscle gets two hard sessions too close together.

sections.heading: About the app's frequency note
body: The app shows an info note when a muscle gets real work on only one day. Treat it as a scheduling idea: splitting sets over two days makes high weekly targets easier to do with good effort.
The weekly total matters far more than the split; a second day is not special in itself.

points.text: Volume-matched analyses found little growth difference between training a muscle once or more often each week.
Moving some sets to a second day is still a sensible fix when one workout is long or a muscle turns yellow or red on the day map.

notes: vol15 rewrite: face-value weekly volume, the day body map colour per muscle per workout, per-workout cap info-only, suggestion buttons.
Pelland 2026 is a meta-regression; its frequency result is about growth with volume matched, not about any one schedule.
The per-session evidence is a preprint plus a conference abstract (not peer-reviewed) and is labelled as such.
